title: Energy and motion

criteria.text: Understand that the useful work is only achieved by a force that is parallel to the direction of motion
Understand and apply the fact that work is the area under a force–distance graph
Understand that the kinetic energy is directly proportional to velocity squared
Apply the formula: $\Delta E_{\text{k}} = E_{\text{k final}} - E_{\text{k initial}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} - \frac{1}{2}mu^{2}$
Understand that in a closed system the total amount of energy remains the same
Apply the formula: $E_{\text{k initial}} + E_{\text{g initial}} = E_{\text{k final}} + E_{\text{g final}}$
Apply the formula: $\eta = \frac{\text{useful energy out}}{\text{total energy in}}$
Understand that the gradient of a force–compression/extension graph is the spring constant and the area under the graph is the elastic potential energy.
Apply the formula for Hooke’s law: $F = -kx$
Understand that the elastic potential energy is directly proportional to the compression/extension squared
Understand that elastic potential energy can be transformed into other types of energy
Be able to describe the energy transformations that occur in vertical and horizontal oscillating springs

An archer fires a bow directly up. In order to do this, they pull the bow back by 25 cm. The bow has a spring constant of 500 N m$^{-1}$ and the arrow has a mass of 18 g.

parts.question: Calculate the force required by the archer to hold the bow in place.
Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the bow when it is pulled back by 25 cm.
Calculate the maximum height achieved by the arrow from the point of its release.
parts.answer:
$E_{\text{s}} - E_{\text{g to raise the arrow 25 cm}} = E_{\text{g}} = mg\Delta h$
$\Delta h = \frac{E_{\text{s}} - E_{\text{g to raise the arrow 25 cm}}}{mg} = \frac{15.6 - (0.018)(9.8)(0.25)}{(0.018)(9.8)} = 88.2\ \text{m (or 88.3 m if 15.625 J is used)}$

review_questions.question:
A pinball machine uses a handle, spring and soft plunger to launch a ball into the machine. This is shown in the diagram below.
A force-compression graph of this spring is shown below.
The same spring mechanism is used to launch a ball up an incline as shown below.
The ball has a mass of 0.150 kg.

parts.question: Calculate the spring constant of this spring.
How much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring when the force on the spring is 30 N?
parts.answer:
$F = kx$
$x = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{30}{400} = 0.075\ \text{m}$
$E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(400)(0.075)^{2} = 1.125\ \text{J}$
Could also use area under the graph

parts.question: If the spring is compressed by 10 cm and then released, what is the velocity of the ball when it reaches the end of the incline?
parts.answer:
$\Delta h = 85\tan 20^\circ = 30.9\ \text{cm}$
$E_{\text{s}} = E_{\text{g}} + E_{\text{k}}$
$\frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = mg\Delta h + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2\left(\frac{1}{2}k\Delta x^{2} - mg\Delta h\right)}{m}}$
$= \sqrt{\frac{2\left(\frac{1}{2}(400)(0.1)^{2} - (0.15)(9.8)(0.309)\right)}{(0.15)}}$
$= 4.54\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

review_questions.question:
Some arcade game designers are manufacturing a spring to launch a ball from a pinball machine. They test the spring by compressing it by varying amounts and placing a pinball of mass 80 g up to the compressed spring. Then they release the spring and measure the speed with which the pinball leaves the spring. They measure the velocity by timing how long it takes the ball to travel 10 cm and then apply the formula $v = \frac{d}{t}$. A diagram of this set-up is shown below.
The designers collect the results shown in columns 1 and 2 of the table.
| Compression (m) | Compression squared (m$^2$) | Velocity (m s$^{-1}$) | Kinetic energy (J) |
| 0.02 | | 2.7 | |
| 0.04 | | 5.5 | |
| 0.06 | | 8.2 | |
| 0.08 | | 11.0 | |

parts.question: Complete the values for the compression squared and the kinetic energy. Round your answers to one decimal place.
Draw a graph of the kinetic energy vs the square of the compression of the spring on a copy of the grid shown below. Include a line of best fit.
Calculate the gradient of the line of best fit of your graph.
parts.answer:
Use two points on your line of best fit, for example:
$\text{Gradient} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{4-1}{(5.4-1.3)\times10^{-3}} = 732\ \text{J m}^{-2}$
A range of 715–775 J m$^{-2}$ is accepted.

parts.question: Use your answer from part c to calculate the spring constant, k, of the spring.
parts.answer:
$E_{\text{k}} = E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$
$k = \frac{2E_{\text{k}}}{x^{2}} = 2\times\text{gradient} = 2\times732 = 1464\ \text{N m}^{-1}$
A range of 1430–1550 N m$^{-1}$ is accepted.

parts.question: One of the designers states that the way they measured velocity is inaccurate. Other than inaccuracies in timing, explain why the measurement of the velocity is inaccurate, state its effect on the predicted values of the spring constant and suggest a way to reduce this error.
parts.answer: The measurement of the velocity is the average velocity. The ball will likely slow down due to friction, which means the average velocity is slower than the initial velocity and the predicted value of the spring constant will be consistently lower than the true value because $E_{\text{s}} = E_{\text{k}}$, $\frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2},$ $k = \frac{v^{2}m}{x^{2}}$; if velocity decreases, the spring constant decreases.

review_questions.question: A person of mass 60 kg climbs a water slide that is 30.5 m tall. At the top of the slide, the person pushes off the railing, giving themselves an initial velocity of 0.56 m s$^{-1}$. Calculate the velocity of the person as they exit the bottom of the water slide. For this question, assume that friction is negligible.

Students hang a mass of 1.0 kg from a spring that obeys Hooke’s law with k = 10 N m$^{-1}$. The spring has an unstretched length of 2.0 m. The mass then hangs stationary at a distance of 1.0 m below the unstretched position (X) of the spring, at Y, as shown at position 6b in the diagram below. The mass is then pulled a further 1.0 m below this position and released so that it oscillates, as shown in position 6c. Assume the gravitational field strength to be 10 N kg$^{-1}$. Note that this diagram is not to scale.
The zero of gravitational potential energy is taken to be bottom point, Z.
The elastic potential energy and gravitational potential energy are plotted on a graph, as shown in the diagram below.

parts.question: Calculate the total energy of the system when the mass is at its lowest point, Z.
parts.answer: 20 J. Kinetic energy is zero, and from the graph, the spring potential energy is 20 J and gravitational potential energy is 0 J.

parts.question: From the data in the graph, calculate the speed of the mass at its midpoint, Y.
parts.answer:
At point Y there is 10 J of gravitational potential energy and 5 J of spring potential energy. Therefore, 20 – 10 – 5 = 5 J of kinetic energy.
$E_{\text{k}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2E_{\text{k}}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(5)}{1}} = 3.16\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

parts.question:
Without making any other changes, the students now pull the mass down to point P, 0.50 m below Y. They release the mass and it oscillates about Y, as shown right.
The students now take the zero of gravitational potential energy to be at P and the zero of elastic potential energy to be at Q. They expect the total energy at P to be equal to the total energy at Q.
They prepare the following table.
| Position | Gravitational potential energy, $E_g$ | Elastic potential energy, $E_s$ | Kinetic energy, $E_k$ |
| Q | $E_g = mgh = 1.0\times10\times1.0 = 10$ J | $E_s = 0$ | $E_k = 0$ |
| P | $E_g = 0$ | $E_s = \frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\times10\times1.0^{2} = 5.0$ J | $E_k = 0$ |
However, their calculation of the total energy ($E_g + E_s + E_k$) at Q (10 J) is different from their calculation of the total energy at P (5.0 J).
Explain the mistake that the students have made.
parts.answer: The student has assumed that $E_{\text{s}}$ was zero at point Q; it should be calculated from the unstretched length, as $E_{\text{s}}$ is proportional to $x^{2}$. This means the change in $E_{\text{s}}$ is not linear.

review_questions.question: A spring fixed at one end and with a mass attached at the other end is placed horizontally on a polished surface that can be considered frictionless. The mass is then pulled, extending the spring, then released and allowed to oscillate freely. Describe the changes to elastic potential energy and kinetic energy that occur as the spring goes from a fully extended to a fully compressed position. The spring works the same in extension and compression.
review_questions.answer: When the spring is extended, the spring potential energy is at a maximum but the kinetic energy is zero. Once released, the spring potential energy will decrease as the kinetic energy increases. When the spring is at its rest length it will have no spring potential energy and the kinetic energy will be at a maximum. After this point, the spring will begin to compress and the kinetic energy will decrease, while the spring potential energy increases. Once fully compressed, the spring potential energy will be a maximum and the kinetic energy will be zero.

review_questions.question: Rob and Sophia have set up an energy transfer experiment. In this experiment, a steel ball, that has a mass of 45 g, is hung from the ceiling via a piece of string and then placed next to a loaded spring. The spring is compressed by 5 cm and is held in place by a force of 0.725 N. When the spring is released, it transfers all of its energy to the steel ball, which swings up in an arc. A diagram of this experimental set-up is shown below.

parts.question: Show that the elastic potential energy of the spring is $1.81\times10^{-2}$ J when it is compressed by 5 cm.
Calculate the velocity of the steel ball once the spring is fully extended. Assume that all of the energy of the spring is transferred to the ball.
Determine the maximum height achieved by the ball.
What is the velocity of the ball at its maximum height? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Zero. As the ball increases in height its kinetic energy is being transformed into gravitational potential energy. The maximum height indicated when all of the kinetic energy has been transformed into gravitational potential energy, and therefore the velocity, must be zero at the maximum height.

parts.question: The students want to double the amount of initial spring potential energy. Rob suggests doubling the compression so that the elastic is compressed by 10 cm. Sophia disagrees and says that the spring need only be compressed to 7 cm. Who is correct? Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Sophia is correct. Spring potential energy is directly proportional to the compression squared (the relationship is not linear). This can be proven mathematically as:
$0.0362 = \frac{1}{2}\times14.5\times x^{2}$
$x = 0.0706\ \text{m or } 7.06\ \text{cm}$

summary:
Chapter 9 Summary

9A Work

How is work calculated?

Work is the amount of energy transferred from one object or system to
another.

Force must be applied parallel to the direction of displacement. If it's
not, find the component of the force that is parallel to the direction
of motion, using trigonometry.

$$W = Fs\ cos\ \theta$$

This may be termed the 'useful work'.

Work may be positive (given to an object) or negative (taken away from
the object)

No work is done when an object is held in a fixed position, as there is
no displacement.

Force--distance graphs

For a constant force y applied over a distance x:

The area under a force-displacement graph is work done, because work =
force × displacement.

In the graph shown the area is xy.

9B Energy, power and energy efficiency

Energy is the measurable property of a body or system with the ability
to do work. Energy can be transformed from one form to another, the same
type of energy can be transferred from one object to another, and energy
cannot be created or destroyed.

Gravitational potential energy

Gravitational potential energy is the amount of energy an object has
stored due to its position in a gravitational field; measured in joules
(J).

Kinetic energy

Remember to use the SI unit for speed or velocity, m s$^{-1}$

This means (for an object of constant mass) kinetic energy is directly
proportional to the square of the velocity.

Energy transformation from one form to another

Motion and energy in systems

System: a collection of objects that can interact with each other

Closed system: a system that does not allow the transfer of mass or
energy to the surrounding environment. In a closed system the total
amount of energy remains the same. When analysing energy and motion we
usually assume the system is closed.

Open system: a system that does allow the transfer of mass or energy to
the surrounding environment. The only type usually considered are
inelastic collisions, where thermal and sound energy is lost to the
surrounds.

Power

Power required to overcome friction and maintain a constant velocity.

P = $Fv_{\text{av}}$

Energy efficiency

Energy efficiency: the ratio of the energy output to the energy input of
a system

9C Springs

Elasticity

Elastic material: a material that can store elastic potential energy and
is able to return to its original shape once the energy is released

Elastic limit: the maximum deformation that can occur without causing
permanent deformation

Ideal spring: a hypothetical spring that is considered frictionless and

Elastic potential energy

The energy needed to extend the spring increases the more lengthened the
spring becomes.

The elastic potential energy for a spring is directly proportional to
